### Observed differences

- For six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22), the resources executing the work changed almost completely. In the earlier window, each activity was handled by a stable group of about ten resources, each contributing roughly 4–10 in 100 assignments — together roughly 53–63 in 100 — with the rest spread over a long tail of minor resources. In the later window, most of these resources no longer appear among the main performers (for example User_16, previously at 6–10 in 100 on these activities, is no longer visible), while a largely different set took over — for example User_97, now among the most-used performers on each of these activities at about 5–9 in 100 — together roughly 35–45 in 100; only one or two of the earlier resources remain visible, at about 4–6 in 100 each. The anonymous tail of minor resources grew from roughly 37–45 in 100 to roughly 47–54 in 100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

- Activity A11 shows the sharpest shift: in the earlier window its assignments were spread over 20 distinct resources, with the largest share (User_115) at about 15 in 100 and a concentration index of 0.07; in the later window all of the roughly 110 traces containing A11 were assigned to User_115 alone — one distinct resource, top share 100 in 100, concentration index 1.0. [ASSIGN003, CONC001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis of a change in resource allocation: the work on seven activities (A01, A03, A11, A13, A14, A17, A22) was reassigned from the group of resources that performed it in the earlier window to a largely different group, with A11 changing from being shared across about 20 resources to being handled exclusively by User_115, which previously held only about 15 in 100 of its assignments. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

Supporting signs: all eight qualifying items come from the resource family, where 8 items were observed against roughly 0.004 expected by chance for the 8 units tested, while control flow (0 of 36 units) and timing (0 of 36) produced none — consistent with a change confined to allocation; all seven activity profiles move in the same direction; each difference exceeds about 1995 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled data; the A11 concentration change is corroborated by a second indicator; and every profile rests on well over 100 traces containing the activity in each window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

Limitations: the profiles show only the ten most-used resources plus an aggregated remainder, and that remainder grew to roughly half of all assignments, so the exact composition of the incoming group — and whether its members were genuinely new or previously hidden in the tail — cannot be read from the evidence; the identical profiles for A13 and A14 suggest the items partly reflect one underlying reassignment rather than independent confirmations; and a shift in the mix of cases reaching these activities cannot be ruled out as the driver of the reallocation. Resource codes are anonymous, so no roles or teams are implied. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]
